summaries.example: Imagine you find a wallet on the playground. You may want to keep the money, but your conscience tells you to return it. Butler would say that wanting something is not the same as having the best guide for action. Thinking carefully about what is fair can help your conscience guide your other feelings.
summaries.summary: Joseph Butler argued that human beings are guided by several different parts of their nature. We have particular wants and feelings, concern for ourselves, care for others, and conscience. Conscience is our ability to think about right and wrong. Butler believed it should have authority over our other motives. This does not mean that caring about ourselves is bad. Proper self-love means seeking our real good, not simply grabbing whatever we want right now. Butler also rejected the idea that every action is secretly selfish. A person can genuinely feel compassion and want to help someone else. Still, our motives are often mixed. We may help partly because we care and partly because we want praise. Butler thought careful reflection was important because people often fool themselves about their reasons. He recommended trying to judge our own actions as we would judge another person’s actions. He also warned that human beings know very little about the larger purposes of the world, so we should focus on understanding our nature and governing our conduct.
key_ideas: People have many feelings and desires, such as wanting pleasure, safety, or praise.
Butler says conscience should guide these feelings, even when another desire feels stronger.
Caring about yourself and caring about others do not have to fight each other.
Our feelings can be mixed, so we need careful thinking about our reasons.
People should examine their choices because it is easy to make excuses for themselves.
Compassion can help us notice and respond to another person’s suffering.
summaries.why_it_matters: Butler’s ideas help us think about everyday choices. A strong feeling is not always the best guide. We can care for ourselves without ignoring other people, and we can care for others without pretending that our own needs do not matter. His warning about self-deceit is useful whenever we are tempted to make an excuse or judge ourselves more gently than we judge someone else. His account of compassion and carefully limited anger also helps explain how kindness and fairness can work together.

important_terms.definition: The inner ability to think about whether an action is right or wrong and to guide our choices.
A desire to protect and improve your own happiness and well-being. Butler says this is different from selfishness.
Care for other people and a wish to help when they are hurting or need support.
A mistake in which we give ourselves excuses and fail to see that our own choices may be wrong.

questions_to_think_about: Have you ever wanted to do something but decided it was not fair?
Why might people make excuses for themselves more easily than for others?
Can helping someone else also make you feel happy?
When might anger help protect people, and when might it go too far?

summaries.example: Suppose a student discovers that a close friend cheated on an exam. Self-partiality may encourage silence, while concern for the friend may make the student want to protect them. Butler’s framework asks the student to distinguish immediate motives from conscience, which evaluates the situation by moral standards. It also allows for mixed motives: reporting the cheating might express concern for fairness, loyalty to other students, fear of consequences, or several of these at once. Reflection should test whether the decision can be defended without relying on a private excuse.
summaries.summary:
Joseph Butler’s moral philosophy begins with a detailed account of human psychology. Human beings contain particular passions and desires, benevolence, self-love, and conscience. Butler distinguishes several meanings of “nature”: a feature found in human beings, the strongest motive within a group, and a principle with authority to organize and govern other motives. His central claim is that moral authority cannot simply be identified with whichever desire is strongest. Conscience is a reflective capacity that assesses conduct as right or wrong and, on Butler’s principal view, has natural supremacy. Interpreters disagree about how this supremacy relates to self-love and benevolence, since Butler sometimes presents these as subordinate to conscience and sometimes gives them a more elevated status. Critics have also questioned whether his argument moves in a circle: does conscience establish natural order, or does an independently defined natural order explain conscience’s authority?

Butler’s account of self-love is aimed partly at Hobbesian or psychological egoist theories. He separates a particular appetite, such as hunger, from self-love, which concerns one’s general happiness. The fact that a person enjoys satisfying a desire does not show that the desire’s object is the person’s own self-interest. Likewise, compassion can be directed toward another’s suffering even when compassionate action also benefits the agent. Butler therefore allows mixed motives without reducing every motive to selfishness. He maintains that properly reflective self-love and benevolence are usually compatible, while recognizing that particular prudential considerations can conflict with conscience.

key_ideas: Butler develops moral philosophy from observations about human nature and action, rather than relying only on abstract, supposedly necessary relations.
He distinguishes three senses of nature: what belongs to human beings, what is strongest among motives, and what has governing authority.
The strongest motive at a moment is not necessarily the motive that ought to govern action; conscience may have authority even when another desire is more powerful.
Butler argues that self-love, properly understood as concern for genuine happiness, is not equivalent to selfishness and can generally support benevolence.
His rejection of psychological egoism depends on distinguishing a passion’s object from the fact that the passion belongs to the person who experiences it.
Compassion is morally important, while resentment can serve justice only when directed at wrongdoing and controlled so that goodwill is not abandoned.
summaries.why_it_matters: Butler offers a framework for analyzing moral conflict without assuming that people have only one kind of motivation. His distinctions help separate immediate desire from considered interest, genuine concern for others from mere reputation-seeking, and justified resentment from revenge. The account of self-deception is especially relevant to moral responsibility: people may know general standards yet distort their application through partiality, selective attention, or convenient advice. important_terms.definition: A reflective capacity that evaluates prospective and past conduct by moral principles and has authority over other motives.
A principle directed toward one’s own happiness, interest, and private good; Butler distinguishes it from particular desires and from selfishness.
Concern for the good or suffering of others, sometimes treated by Butler as a passion and sometimes as a guiding principle.
A theory claiming that human motivation is fundamentally selfish; Butler attacks it partly by distinguishing passions from the principle of self-love.
A system in which different motives have different roles and an authoritative principle governs the others. Butler uses this picture to explain human nature.
A process of mistaking or hiding one’s own motives and conduct, often by avoiding reflection or applying standards more leniently to oneself.
A feeling of sorrow and concern for another’s suffering that can motivate efforts to relieve it.
A response to injustice that can support justice, but must be restrained so that it does not become revenge or malice.

questions_to_think_about: Does Butler successfully establish that conscience has authority, or does his account assume the very authority it needs to justify?
If virtue usually promotes happiness, can conscience still have a distinct role from self-love?
Can a person’s motives be genuinely benevolent if helping others also produces personal satisfaction?
What limits should be placed on resentment when someone has caused serious harm?
How much can moral conclusions be drawn from facts about human nature without a theological account of human purpose?

summaries.example: A student hears that a friend is being left out of a group project. The student wants to help, but also worries about losing popularity. Butler would ask the student to separate these motives instead of calling the whole choice selfish or completely generous. Compassion may point toward helping. Self-love may consider the student’s own relationships and peace of mind. Conscience asks what is fair and responsible. The student should try to judge the situation from the other students’ point of view, not only from the viewpoint that makes the student look best.
summaries.summary:
Joseph Butler’s moral philosophy asks how different parts of human nature fit together. People have particular desires and emotions, concern for their own happiness, concern for others, and conscience. Conscience means the reflective ability to judge actions as right or wrong. Butler argues that it has a special authority: it should guide the other motives rather than simply being pushed aside by the strongest feeling. He compares this to an organized system in which different parts have different jobs. A person may strongly want something and still have reason not to do it.

Butler gives “nature” several meanings. It can mean anything that belongs to human beings, the strongest motive in a situation, or a governing principle that directs other motives. These meanings must not be confused. For example, anger may be powerful, but that does not make it the proper ruler of action. Butler’s account has led philosophers to disagree about whether conscience is clearly distinct from self-love and benevolence, and about whether moral authority follows from human nature alone or depends on theological ideas about human purpose.

A major part of Butler’s work attacks psychological egoism, the theory that everyone is always motivated by selfishness. He distinguishes self-love, which seeks one’s general happiness, from particular desires such as hunger, embarrassment, or the wish for praise. We may enjoy satisfying a desire because it is ours, but that does not prove that the desire is aimed at ourselves. In the same way, compassion can genuinely be directed at another person’s suffering, even though helping may also make us feel satisfied. Butler thinks self-love and benevolence usually fit together, but he allows that local self-interest can sometimes conflict with conscience.

B
key_ideas: Butler studies morality by examining human motives and patterns of action, not only by starting with abstract rules.
He says “nature” can mean what belongs to us, what is strongest, or what ought to govern other motives.
A strong desire is not automatically the right guide. Conscience can have authority even when it is not the strongest feeling.
Self-love and benevolence can usually support each other when they are understood carefully.
Butler rejects the claim that compassion and other outward-looking motives are merely disguised selfishness.
People often deceive themselves by judging their own actions more generously than they judge other people’s actions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Butler’s account is useful for understanding moral disagreements inside one person. We may care about fairness, friendship, comfort, reputation, and other people’s suffering all at once. Instead of pretending that one motive explains everything, his theory encourages us to sort out the motives and ask which should govern. His discussion of self-deceit also gives a practical lesson: compare how we judge ourselves with how we judge others, examine inconvenient facts, and be cautious about convenient excuses. His treatment of compassion, resentment, and forgiveness shows how care for others and opposition to wrongdoing might coexist, while also warning that anger can turn into revenge.

important_terms.definition: The ability to reflect on actions and judge them by ideas of right and wrong. Butler treats it as a guiding authority within human nature.
Concern for one’s own lasting happiness and good. Butler says it should not be confused with grabbing whatever one wants.
Concern for other people’s well-being. Butler sometimes describes it as a feeling and sometimes as a broader principle for action.
The view that all human actions are secretly motivated by self-interest. Butler argues that this confuses having a desire with desiring oneself.
A mistaken process of giving ourselves unfair excuses or avoiding facts so that our choices seem better than they are.
Sorrow and concern for another person’s suffering, together with a wish to reduce it.

questions_to_think_about: Is a choice selfish if it helps someone else and also makes you feel good?
Why does Butler distinguish the strongest motive from the motive that should guide us?
Can anger ever protect fairness instead of becoming revenge?
What habits might help a person notice self-deceit?
Does Butler need religious beliefs to support all of his moral arguments?
